newsitem.title: UK: British water firm may beat drought via Eurotunnel.
newsitem.headline: British water firm may beat drought via Eurotunnel.

text.p: As Britain's driest January for over 200 years drew to an end on Friday, a water company was drawing up contingency plans to bring French water through Channel Tunnel cooling pipes.
The Folkestone and Dover Water Company believes it could use the pipes running through the 50 km (30 mile) tunnel to relieve drought-hit southeastern England.

"(The Channel ports of) Folkestone and Dover have problems because they are in one of the driest parts of the country," Pamela Taylor, chief executive of the Water Companies Association, told BBC radio.
"A contingency plan is the possibility of bringing water through the tunnel," she added.
French water company Generale des Eaux bought a majority stake in Folkestone and Dover Water in 1989.

A spokeswoman for Eurotunnel, the company which owns the tunnel, said that, if the scheme was to be carried out, special work would be necessary to connect the cooling pipes to the French and British water systems.
She said the scheme could not even be considered until the completion of repair work to the tunnel following a fire in November which resulted in the temporary closure of the tunnel.

Weather monitors in Britain reported on Friday that rainfall in England and Wales this month was just 18 percent of the normal 88 mm (2.24 inches), the lowest figure since 1779. Scotland had just 40 percent of average January rainfall.
